description: How to read, write and interpret algorithms using pseudocode and flowcharts.
content_html:
What Is an Algorithm?

An algorithm is a precise, step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem. Every program you have ever run began as an algorithm. Before any code is written, a programmer must first design the logical steps the computer needs to follow. Getting those steps right — in the right order, with the right decisions — is the foundation of good software.

Algorithms are not the same as programs. A program is a specific implementation in a specific language. An algorithm is language-independent — the same logic can be expressed in pseudocode, as a flowchart, or as code in Python, Java or any other language. Your exam tests whether you can design, trace and evaluate algorithms, regardless of which language you prefer to code in.

Key Fact

A good algorithm must be unambiguous (each step has exactly one interpretation), finite (it must eventually stop), and effective (it must actually solve the problem it was designed for).

Pseudocode

Pseudocode is an informal notation that sits halfway between plain English and a real programming language. It is precise enough to be translated directly into code, but readable enough that a non-programmer can follow the logic. Your exam uses a set of specific pseudocode conventions — learn them so your algorithms are unambiguous.

The key pseudocode keywords you need are shown below. Notice how they map to real programming ideas:

PurposePseudocode keywordExample
AssignmentSETSET total = 0
Output to screenOUTPUTOUTPUT “Hello”
Input from userRECEIVERECEIVE name FROM (STRING)
ConditionalIF / ELSE / END IFIF score > 50 THEN
Count-controlled loopFOR / NEXTFOR i = 1 TO 10
Condition-controlled loopWHILE / END WHILEWHILE total < 100
Post-condition loopREPEAT / UNTILREPEAT ... UNTIL done = TRUE
Define subroutinePROCEDURE / END PROCEDUREPROCEDURE greet(name)
Define functionFUNCTION / END FUNCTIONFUNCTION square(n)
Return a valueRETURNRETURN result

Below is a complete pseudocode algorithm that asks the user for three numbers and outputs their average. Each line maps directly to a keyword in the table above.

RECEIVE num1 FROM (INTEGER)
RECEIVE num2 FROM (INTEGER)
RECEIVE num3 FROM (INTEGER)
SET total = num1 + num2 + num3
SET average = total / 3
OUTPUT “The average is ” & average

Notice: RECEIVE handles input, SET handles assignment, and OUTPUT sends text to the screen. The & operator joins (concatenates) a string and a number in the output.

Flowcharts

A flowchart shows exactly the same logic as pseudocode but as a visual diagram. Each shape has a fixed meaning. Arrows show the flow of control — which instruction comes next. You need to know five shapes:

ShapeNameUsed for
Oval / rounded rectangleTerminatorSTART and STOP of the algorithm
RectangleProcessAny calculation, assignment or output step
ParallelogramInput / OutputReceiving data from the user or displaying a result
DiamondDecisionA yes/no question — branches the flow
Rectangle with double side barsSubroutine callCalling a named subroutine or function
Key Fact

Every flowchart must start and end with a terminator (oval). Decision diamonds always have exactly two exit arrows, typically labelled “Yes” and “No”. Process boxes have one entry and one exit arrow.

Many students write Python or JavaScript instead of pseudocode when the exam asks for an algorithm. While examiners usually award marks for logically correct code, there are two risks. First, Python’s print() is not the same as OUTPUT — if your Python is wrong, you score zero. Second, pseudocode is faster to write in exam conditions because you don’t worry about syntax errors.

Another common error is writing prose instead of pseudocode: “Ask the user for a number, add it to the total, and repeat.” This is not pseudocode — it has no control structure keywords and cannot be traced step by step. Always use the keywords: RECEIVE, SET, FOR, WHILE, IF.

Trace Tables

A trace table is used to check an algorithm by simulating it line by line. You create a column for every variable, plus an output column. Then you work through the algorithm and record the value of each variable after each step. Trace-table questions are a regular feature of the written exam — many students give only the final answer and lose intermediate marks.

Consider this algorithm:

SET total = 0
FOR i = 1 TO 3
  SET total = total + i
NEXT i
OUTPUT total

Trace table:

LineitotalOutput
SET total = 0—0
i = 1, total = 0 + 111
i = 2, total = 1 + 223
i = 3, total = 3 + 336
OUTPUT total6

The answer is 6. Fill in every row — marks are awarded per row, not just for the final output.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to “write an algorithm in pseudocode”, use the correct keywords: SET, OUTPUT, RECEIVE, IF/ELSE/END IF, FOR/NEXT, WHILE/END WHILE. Writing Python without being asked is risky — one syntax slip costs marks. For trace-table questions, complete every row — the mark scheme awards a mark for each correct intermediate state, not just the final output.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • An algorithm is a finite, unambiguous set of steps for solving a problem; pseudocode and flowcharts are two standard ways to express one before coding begins.
  • Pseudocode uses keywords such as SET, OUTPUT, RECEIVE, IF, FOR, WHILE, and REPEAT — learn the exact conventions used in your exam.
  • Flowchart shapes have fixed meanings: ovals are terminators, rectangles are processes, parallelograms are input/output, diamonds are decisions, and double-barred rectangles are subroutine calls.

practice_questions.text:
Which flowchart symbol is used to represent a decision in an algorithm?
A) Rectangle
B) Oval
C) Diamond
D) Parallelogram
State the pseudocode keyword used to receive input from a user.

practice_questions.marks: A precise / step-by-step [1] set of instructions for solving a problem [1]. Award both marks for a definition that captures precision and problem-solving purpose.

practice_questions.text:
The algorithm below is intended to output the sum of all whole numbers from 1 to 5.

SET total = 0
FOR i = 1 TO 5
  SET total = total + i
NEXT i
OUTPUT total

Complete a trace table showing the value of i and total after each iteration of the loop.
practice_questions.marks:
Full trace table:
i=1, total=1 [1]
i=2, total=3 [1]
i=3, total=6 [1]
i=4, total=10; i=5, total=15; OUTPUT 15 [1]
Mastering: All rows correct with output 15.
Secure: 3 out of 4 rows correct.
Developing: 2 correct rows.
Emerging: 1 correct row or only final answer given.

practice_questions.text: A student wants to write a pseudocode algorithm that asks a user for their age and outputs 'Adult' if the age is 18 or over, or 'Minor' if it is below 18. Write a pseudocode algorithm to do this.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Write an Algorithm in Pseudocode
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correct RECEIVE, valid IF condition (age >= 18), correct THEN/ELSE branches with matching OUTPUT, END IF present, all keywords correct — 5-6 marks.
Secure: Logic correct but minor keyword inconsistency or missing END IF — 3-4 marks.
Developing: IF condition present but branches or keywords incomplete — 2 marks.
Emerging: Some keywords attempted but logic incorrect — 1 mark.
Model answer:
RECEIVE age FROM (INTEGER)
IF age >= 18 THEN
  OUTPUT "Adult"
ELSE
  OUTPUT "Minor"
END IF

practice_questions.text: A programmer designs a flowchart before writing code. Explain two advantages of designing an algorithm using a flowchart before writing code.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks per advantage (1 for the point, 1 for development):
- Visual representation makes the flow of control easy to follow / easier to spot logic errors before any code is written [1+1].
- Language-independent: the flowchart can be converted into any programming language / a team member unfamiliar with Python can still understand the algorithm [1+1].
- Easier to communicate with non-programmers / clients can review logic without needing to read code [1+1].
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed advantages.
Secure: Two valid advantages, one developed.
Developing: One developed advantage or two simple points.
Emerging: One simple relevant point.

flashcard_questions.a: A precise, step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem.

flashcard_questions.q: What three properties must a good algorithm have?
flashcard_questions.a: It must be unambiguous, finite, and effective.

flashcard_questions.q: What pseudocode keyword assigns a value to a variable?
What pseudocode keyword reads input from the user?
What pseudocode keyword sends output to the screen?
Which flowchart shape represents a decision?
flashcard_questions.a: A diamond, with Yes and No exit arrows.

flashcard_questions.q: Which flowchart shape marks the start and end of an algorithm?
Which flowchart shape is used for an input or output step?
Which flowchart shape represents a call to a subroutine?
flashcard_questions.a: A rectangle with double vertical bars on each side.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a trace table used for?
flashcard_questions.a: To simulate an algorithm step by step, recording each variable's value after every line.

flashcard_questions.q: In a trace table, what must you record beyond the final output?
flashcard_questions.a: The value of every variable after each step, not just the final answer.

flashcard_questions.q: How does pseudocode differ from a real programming language?
flashcard_questions.a: Pseudocode uses plain English keywords and has no strict syntax rules — it cannot be run directly.

glossary_terms.definition: A precise, step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem or carrying out a task.
An informal, structured way of describing an algorithm using plain English mixed with programming-style keywords.
A visual diagram using standard symbols to represent the steps and flow of control in an algorithm.
The order in which instructions in an algorithm are carried out.
